hero.headline: Brother of slain Indian River deputy reacts to Oct. 27 execution date for killer
hero.teaser: Marc Raczkoski said he finally has closure after Gov. Ron DeSantis signed a death warrant for William Reaves, who murdered his brother, Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkoski, in 1986.
hero.body:
Marc Raczkoski said he finally has closure after Gov. Ron DeSantis signed the death warrant for William Reaves, the man convicted of killing his brother, Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkoski, in 1986. The execution is set for Oct. 27.

 "It gives closure," Marc Raczkoski said at his brother's grave at Hillcrest Memorial Gardens in Fort Pierce. "It's finally over."

 Richard Raczkoski was 29 years old when he was shot four times and killed on Nov. 23, 1986, after answering a 911 call at a convenience store in Indian River County. Authorities arrested William Reaves, then 37, days later in Albany, Georgia. Reaves confessed to killing Raczkoski, saying he panicked when a gun fell out of his shorts and that he was under the influence of drugs. Reaves was convicted of murder in 1987 and sentenced to death.

 Marc Raczkoski, who was 22 at the time of his brother's death, said the years without resolution took a toll on his entire family. "No more Christmas trees in the house. Holidays were never the same.

 Mom didn't decorate," he said. He described standing beside his brother's grave for 40 years, waiting and wondering. "Feels like everybody forgot," he said.

 Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers said the execution will bring healing to the agency. "All of that is very heavy on our agency, and knowing that this execution is coming in October gives a little weight lifted off. I think it's going to be a moment of healing for our agency," Flowers said.

 The sheriff said he plans to attend the execution. "Because I want to make sure the last thing he sees is an Indian River County Deputy uniform," Flowers said.

 Reaves has one last chance at an appeal. If carried out, the execution will mark Florida's 18th this year, following 19 executions in 2025. Grace Hanna of Floridians Against the Death Penalty said her organization has raised concerns about the rapid pace of executions and the transparency of the selection process.

 Marc Raczkoski said his brother was always focused on public service and liked to fish and enjoy the outdoors. "He was quick to make you laugh," Marc Raczkoski said. "For what he did to Richard, yes. What he did and the way he did it, yes, it gives me some closure, but still the pain will still always be there."

cards.headline: Card skimmer discovered on 7-Eleven gas pump in Fort Pierce prompts investigation
cards.teaser: A cybersecurity professional found a card skimming device on a gas pump at a 7-Eleven on Orange Avenue in Fort Pierce on Monday morning, prompting a police investigation.
cards.body:
A cybersecurity professional found a card skimming device on a gas pump at a 7-Eleven on Orange Avenue in Fort Pierce on Monday morning, prompting a police investigation. Arlo Bess said he routinely checks for card skimmers before using gas pumps and discovered the device after pulling on the card reader.

 "So, I pulled the card reader out and it took a little bit of pull, a couple pounds of pull because it was just stuck in there. It wasn't much at all, and when I got it, I was at first very surprised," Bess said. "I'm just naturally paranoid, if you would, from all my work and training." After finding the device, he locked his truck and informed the store manager. "She was equally surprised and said she had never seen one before," he added.

 Fort Pierce Police Major Michael Santiago said the department is investigating the incident. "We try to track it back to whoever may own that particular skimmer. We also check our systems to see if there's something going on in the neighboring jurisdictions, if they've had similar incidents," Santiago said.

 "We conducted intense screening of video surveillance from the actual location to try and identify who may have installed this particular device. I can tell you it's a little difficult because we simply don't know when it was installed."

 Card skimmers are devices that criminals attach to legitimate card readers to steal card information, including PINs. "On the inside of that skimmer, it's got a little microchip in there, and typically they'll have like a Bluetooth connectivity piece in there. When you slide your card in there, it actually reads the mag stripe off the card and it will intercept that information," Bess said. He noted that no other gas pumps at the station had card skimmers.

 Santiago and Bess warned that card skimmers can also be found on ATM machines, where criminals may use pinhole cameras to capture PINs. "Typically, if it's an ATM machine, you've got a debit card, and you have a PIN that you have to put in. So, they'll also have these little pin cameras that will take a picture and watch you actually putting your PIN into the ATM machine," Bess said.

 To identify card skimmers, Santiago recommended checking for tamper-evident seals, such as red or orange tape, on gas pumps. "If that seal is broken, don't use the system and alert the tenant," he said. Bess added that visual inspection can sometimes help.

 "Visually, you cannot tell. The other card readers, if you look at them on the gas pump, the original ones and even the original one on that one, they'll be slightly dirty, slightly dinged up a little bit," he said.

 Santiago advised paying for gas inside the store or using tap-to-pay at the pump to avoid potential skimmers. If investigators find the person responsible, that individual will face charges of fraud. "Depending on what we find, if we can connect how much money was actually stolen from this particular skimmer, there's always some charges that we can address when it comes to that point," Santiago said.

cards.headline: More than 1,000 volunteers turn out for Martin County beach cleanup
cards.teaser: More than 1,000 volunteers participated in a beach cleanup throughout Martin County on Saturday as part of the International Coastal Cleanup.
cards.body:
More than 1,000 volunteers participated in a beach cleanup throughout Martin County on Saturday as part of the International Coastal Cleanup. Keep Martin Beautiful coordinated the local effort across 28 locations.

 The nonprofit, volunteer-based community action organization was founded in 1994 as an affiliate of Keep America Beautiful. County volunteers participated at Stuart Beach, Hobe Sound Beach, Jensen Beach, Jensen Causeway, Bob Graham Beach, Sandsprit Park, and Indian Riverside Park.

 Keep Martin Beautiful said the cleanup helps protect birds and marine life by reducing the likelihood that these creatures will become injured or entangled in plastics or ingest deadly debris.

 Linda Emerson participated at Blowing Rocks Preserve on Jupiter Island. She said picking up pieces of plastic allows people to realize how much they are using in their own lives and choose to make a difference.

cards.headline: Brother of slain Indian River deputy reacts to Oct. 27 execution date for killer
cards.teaser: Marc Raczkoski said he finally has closure after Gov. Ron DeSantis signed a death warrant for William Reaves, who murdered his brother, Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkoski, in 1986.
cards.body:
Marc Raczkoski said he finally has closure after Gov. Ron DeSantis signed the death warrant for William Reaves, the man convicted of killing his brother, Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkoski, in 1986. The execution is set for Oct. 27.

 "It gives closure," Marc Raczkoski said at his brother's grave at Hillcrest Memorial Gardens in Fort Pierce. "It's finally over."

 Richard Raczkoski was 29 years old when he was shot four times and killed on Nov. 23, 1986, after answering a 911 call at a convenience store in Indian River County. Authorities arrested William Reaves, then 37, days later in Albany, Georgia. Reaves confessed to killing Raczkoski, saying he panicked when a gun fell out of his shorts and that he was under the influence of drugs. Reaves was convicted of murder in 1987 and sentenced to death.

 Marc Raczkoski, who was 22 at the time of his brother's death, said the years without resolution took a toll on his entire family. "No more Christmas trees in the house. Holidays were never the same.

 Mom didn't decorate," he said. He described standing beside his brother's grave for 40 years, waiting and wondering. "Feels like everybody forgot," he said.

 Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers said the execution will bring healing to the agency. "All of that is very heavy on our agency, and knowing that this execution is coming in October gives a little weight lifted off. I think it's going to be a moment of healing for our agency," Flowers said.

 The sheriff said he plans to attend the execution. "Because I want to make sure the last thing he sees is an Indian River County Deputy uniform," Flowers said.

 Reaves has one last chance at an appeal. If carried out, the execution will mark Florida's 18th this year, following 19 executions in 2025. Grace Hanna of Floridians Against the Death Penalty said her organization has raised concerns about the rapid pace of executions and the transparency of the selection process.

 Marc Raczkoski said his brother was always focused on public service and liked to fish and enjoy the outdoors. "He was quick to make you laugh," Marc Raczkoski said. "For what he did to Richard, yes. What he did and the way he did it, yes, it gives me some closure, but still the pain will still always be there."

hero.body:
More than 1,000 volunteers participated in a beach cleanup throughout Martin County on Saturday as part of the International Coastal Cleanup. Keep Martin Beautiful coordinated the local effort across 28 locations.

 The nonprofit, volunteer-based community action organization was founded in 1994 as an affiliate of Keep America Beautiful. County volunteers participated at Stuart Beach, Hobe Sound Beach, Jensen Beach, Jensen Causeway, Bob Graham Beach, Sandsprit Park, and Indian Riverside Park.

 Keep Martin Beautiful said the cleanup helps protect birds and marine life by reducing the likelihood that these creatures will become injured or entangled in plastics or ingest deadly debris.

 Linda Emerson participated at Blowing Rocks Preserve on Jupiter Island. She said picking up pieces of plastic allows people to realize how much they are using in their own lives and choose to make a difference.

cards.headline: Card skimmer discovered on 7-Eleven gas pump in Fort Pierce prompts investigation
cards.teaser: A cybersecurity professional found a card skimming device on a gas pump at a 7-Eleven on Orange Avenue in Fort Pierce on Monday morning, prompting a police investigation.
cards.body:
A cybersecurity professional found a card skimming device on a gas pump at a 7-Eleven on Orange Avenue in Fort Pierce on Monday morning, prompting a police investigation. Arlo Bess said he routinely checks for card skimmers before using gas pumps and discovered the device after pulling on the card reader.

 "So, I pulled the card reader out and it took a little bit of pull, a couple pounds of pull because it was just stuck in there. It wasn't much at all, and when I got it, I was at first very surprised," Bess said. "I'm just naturally paranoid, if you would, from all my work and training." After finding the device, he locked his truck and informed the store manager. "She was equally surprised and said she had never seen one before," he added.

 Fort Pierce Police Major Michael Santiago said the department is investigating the incident. "We try to track it back to whoever may own that particular skimmer. We also check our systems to see if there's something going on in the neighboring jurisdictions, if they've had similar incidents," Santiago said.

 "We conducted intense screening of video surveillance from the actual location to try and identify who may have installed this particular device. I can tell you it's a little difficult because we simply don't know when it was installed."

 Card skimmers are devices that criminals attach to legitimate card readers to steal card information, including PINs. "On the inside of that skimmer, it's got a little microchip in there, and typically they'll have like a Bluetooth connectivity piece in there. When you slide your card in there, it actually reads the mag stripe off the card and it will intercept that information," Bess said. He noted that no other gas pumps at the station had card skimmers.

 Santiago and Bess warned that card skimmers can also be found on ATM machines, where criminals may use pinhole cameras to capture PINs. "Typically, if it's an ATM machine, you've got a debit card, and you have a PIN that you have to put in. So, they'll also have these little pin cameras that will take a picture and watch you actually putting your PIN into the ATM machine," Bess said.

 To identify card skimmers, Santiago recommended checking for tamper-evident seals, such as red or orange tape, on gas pumps. "If that seal is broken, don't use the system and alert the tenant," he said. Bess added that visual inspection can sometimes help.

 "Visually, you cannot tell. The other card readers, if you look at them on the gas pump, the original ones and even the original one on that one, they'll be slightly dirty, slightly dinged up a little bit," he said.

 Santiago advised paying for gas inside the store or using tap-to-pay at the pump to avoid potential skimmers. If investigators find the person responsible, that individual will face charges of fraud. "Depending on what we find, if we can connect how much money was actually stolen from this particular skimmer, there's always some charges that we can address when it comes to that point," Santiago said.
